chapter_theme: Under the heading இன்னா செய்யாமை, eight verses on not hurting others: harm returns on the one who causes it whatever the victim does (43, 46), the self-measure of pain answers the sense of the other as different (44), the scorned dependant and the defenceless strike back by bite or by tears (45, 47), the great cannot be pinched like stone (48), and the worthy do not retaliate against the base, as beneath them and as a waste of their strength (49, 50).

43.reading: One should not hurt anyone at all on the thought that they will bear it, since even for the gods and for those of steadfast love there is no escaping pain for one who makes others suffer.
43.nuance: The verse closes the excuse that the victim's forbearance licenses the harm: the other's patience does not cancel the rebound on the one who hurts. Line 3 is hard to construe: தேவர்க்கும் and திண்ணன்பினார்க்கேயும் may name those to whom the proverb applies (no one, not even gods, is exempt) or those one must not hurt even when they would forgive; the reading takes the first, and கைகூட is left loosely rendered. The address பூவுட்கும் கண்ணாய் (you whose eyes flowers fear) is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: for one who makes others ache there is no freedom from ache

story.act: no story; the proverb states the rebound of pain as a rule that binds even gods and the steadfast

pazhamozhi.applied_to: hurting someone because they will forgive still brings pain back on the one who hurts

44.reading: With no gain to be had from the act and only a sense of the other as different from oneself, one must not deliberately do what makes others tremble, for what is painful to oneself is painful to others.
44.nuance: வேற்றுமை கொண்டு names the cause the proverb answers: treating the other as unlike oneself is what lets one hurt them, and the proverb denies the difference by making one's own pain the measure of theirs. வினைப்பயன் ஒன்றின்றி marks the case as gratuitous harm, with nothing even gained by it. The address to a woman likened to a flowering branch is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: what is painful to oneself is painful to others

story.act: no story; the proverb is the self-measure applied to anyone who would harm another for no purpose

pazhamozhi.applied_to: gratuitous harm rests on a false sense that others feel differently from oneself

45.reading: One should not, judging by appearances that they are powerless, scorn and torment even one's own people who have come to depend on one, for a dog shut in and beaten by a master who does not care for it will bite him.
45.nuance: The verse names the dependants (அடைந்த தமர்) as the victims and the master's belief in their weakness as the error; the proverb shows the weakness is only apparent, and the detail of the shut door (கடையடைத்து) makes cornering the cause of the bite. The proverb's opening quotation mark falls at line 3 and there is no closing mark; போற்றான் at the end of line 2 belongs to the image (the uncaring owner) though it stands outside the marks.
45.domain_note: the head of a house toward kin and dependants

pazhamozhi.proverb: கடையடைத்து வைத்துப் புடைத்தக்கால் நாயும் உடையானைக் கவ்வி விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: if one shuts a door on it and beats it, even a dog will bite its owner

story.act: a master who does not care for his dog shuts it in, beats it, and is bitten

pazhamozhi.applied_to: dependants scorned as powerless will turn on the one who torments them

46.reading: The poet tells his heart that it cannot see what lies far ahead and has surely spoken a cruel thing, for he who looks on another's ruin in the forenoon sees his own ruin in the afternoon.
46.nuance: The verse is addressed to one's own heart, so the cruelty rebuked is an intention or a wish voiced inwardly, not yet a deed; the proverb's கண்டான் (saw) also stops short of doing, and fits one who looks on or wishes for another's ruin. நீயொளியை in line 1 and அடியுளே in line 2 are obscure; the reading takes அடியுளே loosely as 'at the root' (in the end) and leaves நீயொளியை unrendered.

pazhamozhi.proverb: முற்பகல் கண்டான் பிறன்கேடு தன்கேடு பிற்பகல் கண்டு விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: one who saw another's ruin in the forenoon will see his own ruin in the afternoon

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the speaker's own heart, which has voiced a cruel wish

pazhamozhi.applied_to: even a cruel thought toward another returns as one's own ruin, and soon

47.reading: When the strong torment those who are ill-favoured in looks, those without support, the poor, and those they count enemies over a word, the tears the victims weep, unable to bear it, fall on the strong as Death.
47.nuance: The verse names four kinds of the defenceless, one of them (மாற்றத்தால் செற்றார், those taken as foes for a retort) defenceless only because the strong have chosen to treat a word as enmity. The tears are made the agent of the strong man's death, with no king or god named as the one who punishes.

pazhamozhi.proverb: ஆற்றாது அவரழுத கண்ணீர் அவையவர்க்குக் கூற்றமாய் வீழ்ந்து விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: the tears they wept, unable to bear it, fall upon them as Death

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the strong who torment four kinds of the weak

pazhamozhi.applied_to: oppressing the defenceless brings death on the oppressor through his victims' tears

48.reading: To say one will try to bring down those who have much and are held in high esteem is a fault, even if it looks easy, for no one ever pinched a stone off a cold mountain and came away with his hand unhurt.
48.nuance: நற்கெளி தாகி விடினும் concedes that the attack may look easy, and the proverb explains why the look deceives: the mountain does nothing, the hand is hurt by its own act against something harder than itself. The target is the great in means and repute, not necessarily the virtuous.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one has pinched at stone and kept the hand whole

story.act: no story; the proverb's image of pinching rock on a cold hill is applied to anyone who sets out to bring the great low

pazhamozhi.applied_to: attacking the established great harms the attacker, however easy it seems

49.reading: If people lacking worth, out of their own incompleteness, torment the worthy, it is not the way of the worthy to torment them back in anger, for when a dog runs up angered and bites, no one has ever bitten the dog back.
49.nuance: The ground of forbearance is rank, not compassion: the offender is likened to a dog, and retaliating would mean doing what a dog does. கோள் names non-retaliation as the settled stand of the worthy. Line 2's கூர்த்தவரை may mean the worthy are 'keen' or that they 'grow sharp' (angered); the reading takes the second, with the worthy as subject of நலிதல்.

pazhamozhi.literal: if a dog bites, no one bites the dog back

story.act: no story; the dog that runs up and bites stands for the unworthy who torment the worthy

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy do not answer the harm of the base in kind

50.reading: The poet tells a man with a garlanded chest that for the superior to take to heart the wrongs done by the low, who do not keep their hands free of stain, and to rise against them in return is like taking up a fine great weapon against a little jackal.
50.nuance: Where 49 says retaliation is beneath the worthy, this verse says it is waste: the great means of the superior are spent on a target too small to deserve them. The proverb's நல்லா நாராயம் is obscure; it may name a fine iron arrow (நாராசம்) or a mighty weapon, and the reading keeps only the sense of a great weapon used on a small creature. The address காழார மார்ப suggests a man of rank, perhaps a king, though the counsel is general.
50.domain_note: addressed to a man of rank, the counsel for any superior

pazhamozhi.literal: taking up a fine great weapon for a little jackal

story.act: no story; the image of a great weapon spent on a small jackal is applied to the superior who avenges the faults of the low

pazhamozhi.applied_to: answering the faults of the low wastes the strength of the great on what is unworthy of it

links.note: Kural 320 says all pains rest on those who caused pain; Pazhamozhi 43 uses the same word, நோய், in its proverb and applies it to the man who hurts someone because they will forgive.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the rebound of pain is independent of the victim's response: forgiveness on one side does not stop the return of pain on the other.
links.list_adds: it names the excuse the couplet does not, that the victim will bear it, and makes gods and the steadfast fall under the same rule.

links.note: Kural 316 forbids doing to another what one has felt to be painful; Pazhamozhi 44 gives the same self-measure as its proverb and names what blocks it, the sense of the other as different (வேற்றுமை).
links.teaches: Read together, the self-measure of pain is the remedy and the sense of otherness is the disease: the Kural gives the rule, Pazhamozhi names what makes people break it.
links.list_adds: it adds the cause of the harm, a felt difference from the other, and narrows the case to harm with no gain at all.

links.note: Naladiyar 213 holds up the dog that wags its tail with its master's spear in its body as the loyal friend; Pazhamozhi 45 says even a dog shut in and beaten bites its owner.
links.teaches: The same animal marks the limit of loyalty: the Naladiyar praises the dog's endurance of injury, Pazhamozhi shows that cornering and steady abuse break even that endurance.
links.list_adds: its proverb adds the condition, the shut door and repeated beating, under which the quatrain's model of loyal endurance fails.

links.note: Both proverbs of this heading turn on a dog's bite: in 45 the abused dog bites its master, in 49 the worthy man does not bite back the dog that bites him.
links.teaches: The heading uses the dog from both sides, as the weak who will strike back when cornered and as the base whom the worthy will not answer, so the same bite warns the strong and restrains the worthy.

links.note: Kural 319 says hurts done to others in the forenoon come back in the afternoon; Pazhamozhi 46's proverb keeps the forenoon and afternoon but has the man only see (கண்டான்) another's ruin, and addresses the heart.
links.teaches: Together they move the rebound from the deed to the inner wish: the Kural times the return of harm done, Pazhamozhi applies the same timing to a cruel thought voiced in the heart.
links.list_adds: addressing the rebuke to the heart and using 'saw' for 'did' extends the couplet's rule from acts to wishes.

links.note: Kural 204 says that if one plots another's ruin, virtue plots the ruin of the plotter; Pazhamozhi 46 says one who looks on another's ruin sees his own soon after, and rebukes the heart for a cruel word.
links.teaches: Both make inner intent enough to set the return in motion, but the Kural names virtue as the agent while Pazhamozhi names no agent and only the speed of the return.
links.list_adds: it sets the counsel inside a dialogue with one's own heart and swaps the Kural's agent, அறம், for a bare law of time.

links.note: Kural 555 makes the tears of those who cannot bear their affliction the weapon that wears away a ruler's wealth; Pazhamozhi 47 uses the same phrase of tears wept unable to bear it, and makes them Death to any strong oppressor.
links.teaches: Read together, the victims' tears pass from wearing down a king's wealth to killing the oppressor, and from the king's subjects to four named kinds of the defenceless anyone strong might torment.
links.list_adds: it lists four kinds of victims, the ill-favoured, the friendless, the poor and those taken as foes for a word, where the couplet names none.

links.note: Kural 894 says the weak doing harm to the strong is beckoning Death; Pazhamozhi 47 says the strong tormenting the weak find the victims' tears fall on them as Death.
links.teaches: The pair makes Death the outcome on both sides of an unequal fight: the weak who strike the strong invite it by their act, the strong who strike the weak receive it from their victims' tears.
links.list_adds: it reverses the couplet's direction, making the strong the doer and the weak's tears, not the strong man's arm, the bearer of Death.

links.note: Kural 892 says disregard of the great brings ills through the great, with the conduct itself as agent; Pazhamozhi 48's image of the hand hurt by pinching rock makes the same point that the great need not act.
links.teaches: The proverb's mountain gives the couplet's grammar an image: the great do nothing and the attacker's hand is hurt by its own act against something harder, however easy the attack looks.
links.list_adds: it adds the apparent ease of the attack (நற்கெளி தாகி விடினும்) and a proverb that shows why the ease deceives.

links.note: Naladiyar 70 and Pazhamozhi 49 share the proverb that no one bites back a dog that bites; the Naladiyar applies it to low words, Pazhamozhi to harm done (நலிதல்).
links.teaches: The shared proverb carries non-retaliation from insult to injury: the Naladiyar asks the high not to answer low words, Pazhamozhi asks the worthy not to answer actual torment.
links.list_adds: it moves the proverb from speech to deed and names the offender's lack of worth (நீர்த்தகவு இல்லார்) as the reason the worthy hold back.

links.note: Kural 312 says not hurting in return even those who hurt in hatred is the stand (கோள்) of the stainless; Pazhamozhi 49 uses the same word, கோள், for the worthy's refusal to retaliate but grounds it in the offender's likeness to a dog.
links.teaches: The two give the same rule different grounds: the Kural states non-retaliation as purity of the stainless, Pazhamozhi bases it on the offender's lowness, so the restraint becomes a mark of rank.
links.list_adds: its proverb ranks the offender with a dog, a contempt the couplet does not express, and limits the case to offenders lacking worth.

links.note: Kural 158 says those who wrong one out of excess are to be defeated by one's own rightness; Pazhamozhi 50 says the superior should not rise against the low who wrong him at all, since it is a great weapon spent on a jackal.
links.teaches: The couplet still frames forbearance as a way of winning, while Pazhamozhi treats the contest with the low as not worth entering, so forbearance becomes economy of the superior's strength rather than victory.
links.list_adds: its proverb sets a measure of proportion, great means against a small target, that the couplet's language of victory does not.

links.note: Both verses forbid the worthy to answer the low in kind; 49 says it is not their way, 50 says it wastes their strength.
links.teaches: Side by side the two give two separate reasons for the same restraint: retaliation would lower the worthy to the dog's act (49), and it would spend great means on a little jackal (50).

source_issues: 45 lines 3-4: the proverb's quotation opens at கடையடைத்து but has no closing mark, and போற்றான் (the uncaring owner) at the end of line 2 stands outside it though it belongs to the image.
46 line 1: நீயொளியை is obscure as printed and may be a misdivision.
50 line 4: நல்லாநா ராயம் is obscure; the division of the words, and whether நாராயம் is a weapon, cannot be fixed from the text.
